newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe unfolds long-awaited privatisation scheme.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe unfolds long-awaited privatisation scheme.

text.p: Zimbabwe's government has started to unfold a long-awaited privatisation programme in a bid to raise investor interest in the southern African country, officials and economic analysts said on Wednesday.

The government made its first privatisation sale six weeks ago -- floating off dairy company Dairibord -- more than seven years after its first announcement that it would embark on a "vigorous commercialisation and privatisation programme".
Investor interest has not been daunted by the long wait if a 10 times subscription for shares in Dairibord is any measure.
"That is a real indicator of of both local and foreign investor interest," said Nicholas Ncube, the director of the state Zimbabwe Investment Centre (ZIC).

But John Robertson, a leading Zimbabwean private economic consultant, said investor interest could only be sustained if President Robert Mugabe's 17-year-old government abandoned its hesistant approach.
"Investors anywhere in the world need fairly predictable policies and governments which show they are bold and in total control of economic programmes," he told Reuters.
"Our government still has to show that."
For years, the government has been saying the privatisation programme was being delayed because it wanted it to run alongside a campaign to economically empower Zimbabwe's poor majority black people.
Last week, Mugabe told a congress of local industrialists that was still the objective, but pledged to speed up the process.
In the last few weeks state officials have been spelling out timetables for the privatisation of some state enterprises. These are:
Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe (CBZ):
Bank chairman Nicholas Vingirayi says he hopes CBZ would have been privatised by September 1997.

The government would retain 20 percent of the shareholding with 26 percent going to a National Investment Trust that warehouses shares for eventual sale to local black-owned firms, 21 percent going to quasi-government insurance firms, local investors being offered six percent and foreign investors 25 percent.
Cotton Company of Zimbabwe (Cottco):

The state cotton company will be privatised in September 1997, although details of this are still unavailable. The government has appointed Zimbabwe banks, First Merchant Bank and Trust Merchant Bank, and Edwards Financial Services to act as financial advisors.
Stock brokers handling the deal are Kingdom Stockbrokers, Quincors Oames Capel and Edwards and Company.
Zimbabwe Iron Steel Company (ZISCO):

Industry and Commerce Minister Nathan Shamuyarira says the government will give up 70 percent of its shareholding in ZISCO when it privatises the company after completing at the end of 1998 a U.S.$193 million rehabilitation due to start next month.
Air Zimbabwe:

The government says the wholly state-owned national carrier will be privatised once its newly hired Irish chief executive Brendon Donohoe has turned it into a commercial enterprise under his 24-month contract.
But while the government is disinvesting in some companies, it is also seeking to buy up minority shares in two leading mining houses, Lonrho Mining and Anglo American Zimbabwe.
It has signed an agreement in principle to buy a 22 percent stake in Anglo's Bindura Nickel Corporation and is negotiating to buy about half of Lonrho's mining interests in Zimbabwe.
The government says it intends to eventually sell its shares from both deals to black Zimbabweans as part of its economic empowerment programme.
